subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Baked Coffee: The Silent Defect
description: A quick win: understand Baked Coffee: The Silent Defect.

hook.text: Baked coffee looks fine. It smells okay. But the cup is flat, lifeless, and dull. It's the hardest defect to diagnose.

buildup.text: Baking happens when temperature stalls or rises too slowly during the roast. The rate of rise flattens or even dips.

discovery.text: Without momentum, Maillard reactions slow down. Flavors develop incompletely—like bread pulled from the oven too early.

twist.text: Baked coffee is extremely common. Many commercial roasters produce it without realizing because it passes basic quality checks.

climax.text: The fix is ensuring a steady, declining RoR through the roast—never letting momentum stall, especially after first crack.

punchline.text: It looks roasted. It smells roasted. But the cup is dead. That's baking.

quiz.question: What causes 'baked' coffee?
options: Temperature stalling or rising too slowly—rate of rise flattens

details.summary: Baked coffee results when the roast stalls or the rate of rise flattens during development. The beans reach the right color but lack sweetness, complexity, and aromatic intensity. It is called a silent defect because the beans look fine but taste flat and papery.
details.whyItMatters: Baking is the most common hidden roast defect in specialty coffee. Identifying it prevents roasters from shipping bland coffee that looks correct on paper.
takeaways: Baking occurs when rate of rise flattens or stalls mid-roast
Beans look properly roasted but taste flat and dull
Maintaining momentum through development prevents baking

faq.question: How can a cupper identify baked coffee in a tasting session?
faq.answer: Baked coffee typically tastes flat, papery, or bread-like with very little sweetness or acidity. The aroma is muted and the aftertaste fades quickly compared to a well-developed roast of the same bean.

faq.question: What causes the rate of rise to stall and produce baked coffee?
faq.answer: Common causes include dropping the gas too aggressively after first crack, overloading the roaster beyond its capacity, or failing to compensate for the exothermic energy released during development.
